rejected.title: Nutritional imbalance
card: Nutritional imbalance means the foods a person eats do not match what the body needs. It can be too little of some foods, too much of others, or both.
Too little
Many Australians eat too little fruit, vegetables, dairy foods and fibre. These foods supply vitamins, minerals, calcium and fibre.
Too much
Many Australians eat too much fat, salt and sugar. These are often found in processed foods, takeaway meals and sugary drinks.
Over time, nutritional imbalance can raise the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers and tooth decay. It can also contribute to excess body weight.
rejected.remember: Too little, too much or both: any mismatch with the body's needs can raise the risk of disease over time.

a.q: Which description is an example of nutritional imbalance?
opts: Eating few vegetables and often eating salty takeaway
Eating a wide range of foods in sensible amounts
Eating plenty of fibre and drinking mostly water
Eating dairy foods and fruit every day
a.why: Eating few vegetables means too little of a needed food, and salty takeaway means too much salt. The foods do not match what the body needs. The other options describe eating that meets the body's needs.
a.clue: Which option has a mismatch with what the body needs?

b.q: Sam is 17 and eats little fruit or fibre. Most days he has sugary drinks and hot chips. Which change would fix both parts of his imbalance?
opts: Swap sugary drinks for water and eat fruit each day
Keep sugary drinks but take a daily fibre supplement
Cut out dairy foods so that he eats less fat each day
Swap hot chips for salty crisps from a packet each day
b.why: Sam eats too little fruit and fibre and too much sugar and fat, so a fix must add the first and cut the second. Swapping sugary drinks for water and adding fruit does both. A fibre supplement helps only the too little part and leaves the sugar. Cutting dairy removes a food many Australians already eat too little of.
b.clue: Sam has a too little part and a too much part.
